title: Structure padding, alignment and object representation
learningObjectives: Explain why implementations may insert padding between structure members.
Use sizeof to measure the complete structure object size.
Use offsetof to inspect a member offset portably within a given implementation.
Explain why raw structure bytes are not a portable serialization format.
Avoid assuming structure layout or padding values across compilers and platforms.

understand.concept: Implementations may insert padding between structure members and at the end of a structure to satisfy alignment requirements. sizeof includes this padding, and offsetof from stddef.h reports a member offset for the implementation being used. The object representation is not automatically a portable file or network format because padding, byte order and member representations can vary.
understand.whyItMatters: Assuming a fixed structure layout can break binary compatibility across compilers, architectures and build options. Portable serialization should encode fields explicitly.
understand.analogy: Treat each object or stream as a resource with a defined lifetime and explicit rules for access.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal object, storage-duration, alignment or library rules.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Alignment

Some object types have alignment requirements. The implementation can insert padding so members are placed at suitable offsets.

## 2. Structure size

`sizeof(struct Record)` measures the complete structure object, including internal and trailing padding. It is not necessarily the sum of the member sizes.

## 3. Member offsets

Include `<stddef.h>` and use `offsetof(struct Record, member)` to obtain a member's byte offset for the current implementation.

## 4. Portability limits

Different implementations may choose different padding and alignment. Endianness and member representations can also differ, so writing a structure's raw bytes does not define a portable file format.

## 5. Serialize fields explicitly

For portable storage or network protocols, define field widths, byte order, encoding and versioning. Convert each field to and from that specified representation.
